title: Zašto je teško?
theme: English keeps the word still. Bosnian dresses it again.
reviewerNotes: Shorter orientation chapter. Prose uses thesis, support, summary. Spoken lines have cast speakers.

whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: This chapter explains why Bosnian words keep changing their last letters when English words stay still. You may already know Ana’s Book 1 line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. That line is the same drink as kahva, with a different ending because the job in the sentence changed. When you close the laptop you should know where the work lives. English hides grammar in little words, and Bosnian hides it on the end of the noun.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because it keeps the word coffee the same in every job. You can say this is coffee and I want coffee without touching a single letter. Bosnian does not allow that trick. The list word kahva becomes kahvu when Ana wants the drink, because the grammar sits on the end of the word instead of in little words like the and to.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already gave you a line you can say without a chart, and this book is the chart behind it. Ana wants coffee, so she says Želim kahvu instead of repeating the list word kahva. Today you only need the shock that the word changed. Tomorrow you will learn the piles that pick the new ending.
knownLine.speaker: Ana

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: A vocab list shows only one outfit for each noun, and that outfit is the dictionary form. Kahva, most, and kuća are the forms you will see in a list. Real sentences dress those words again when the job changes, so kahva can become kahvu. English never asked you to watch the end of coffee, and that is why the moving letter feels unfair until you expect it.

howYouGuess.heading: How to use this book
howYouGuess.body: Use this book one system at a time, with a small chart, a few tries, and a check. The same coffee, bridge, house, Ana, and Emir come back in every chapter so you are not memorizing a new grocery list. You can start here without finishing Book 1, and the sentences will still make sense. If you already walked Book 1, you get a bonus because you have already said the line.

trick.heading: What we skip
trick.body: This book skips the tourist walk on purpose so the notebook can stay on the endings. There are no civic notes and no cat plot here, because Book 1 already owns that walk through town. We will name a case when a chapter needs a handle, such as nominative or accusative, and we will say the Bosnian name once. Then we move on with the same small set of words.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body: English used to hang grammar on the end of the noun too, back in Old English. Those endings wore off, and word order plus little words like the took the job. Bosnian never fired the endings. Linguists call English analytic now and Bosnian synthetic, but you only need the habit. English moved the work off the noun, and Bosnian left it on.

items.prompt: In English, does coffee change when you want it?
items.explanation: I want coffee uses the same word as this is coffee.

items.prompt: In Želim kahvu, did kahva stay kahva?
items.explanation: It became kahvu because the job in the sentence changed.

items.prompt: Where does Bosnian put the grammar?
options: On the end of the word
items.explanation: The last letters move. English put the work in words like the and to.

items.prompt: The vocab list shows kahva. Is that the only form?
items.explanation: Želim kahvu is the same drink in a different outfit.
Book 1 stays the story. Book 2 stays the later sequel. This is grammar.

questions.question: Why does Bosnian feel harder than English at first?
options: Grammar sits on the end of the word
Every sentence needs a new vocab list
You must learn three languages at once
questions.explanation: English hid the work in little words. Bosnian left it on the noun.

questions.question: What is kahva in a vocab list?
options: The only form you will ever say
questions.explanation: Želim kahvu is the same word doing a different job.

questions.question: In English, I want coffee uses the same coffee as this is coffee. What did Bosnian do?
options: It switched to a new drink
It moved the verb to the end
questions.explanation: Kahva became kahvu. Chapter 1 is why that ending was the she-pile one.

questions.question: What does this book skip on purpose?
options: The walk through town, civic notes, and the cat plot
questions.explanation: Book 1 keeps the walk. This book keeps the notebook.

questions.question: English used to put grammar on the end too. What happened?
options: The endings wore off. Word order and the took the job.
questions.explanation: Bosnian kept the endings. That is the whole headache, and the whole system.

questions.question: What comes next?
questions.explanation: You file the word first. Then the ending can be right.

next.body: You now know that the word will change when the job changes. Chapter 1 files coffee into a pile so the later ending can be the right one. That pile is why kahva is a she.
